en: Saṁyutta Nikāya 20.1 (SN 20.1, PTS SN ii 262) 1. Opamma-vagga Kūṭa-sutta “Bhikkhus, suppose there were a mountain peak as high as Sineru, king of mountains, and a man would come along bringing a wisp of cotton wool. Then he would think: ‘I shall wear away this mountain peak as high as Sineru, king of mountains, with this wisp of cotton wool, rubbing it once every hundred years. Bhikkhus, that mountain peak as high as Sineru, king of mountains, would be worn away sooner than that person would reach the end of old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair through the wearing away of the mass of suffering. Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We will wear away the mass of suffering, the mass of old age and death. It is in this way that you should train yourselves.”
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One ... [as above] ... said this:
“Bhikkhus, just as, for example, whatever rafters there are in a peaked house, they all lead to the peak, converge at the peak, and are destroyed by the destruction of the peak;
even so, bhikkhus, whatever unwholesome states there are, they all have ignorance as their root, converge upon ignorance, and are destroyed by the destruction of ignorance.
Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus:”
‘We shall dwell heedfully.
In this way, monks, you should train yourselves. Thus ends the first [sutta].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 20.2 (SN 20.2, PTS SN ii 263) 1. Opamma-vagga Nakhasikha-sutta (The Finger-Nail) At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, suppose a man were to take up a single grain of dust from the tip of his fingernail and say: ‘The great earth is as much as this grain of dust on the tip of my fingernail, and not more. Now, bhikkhus, would that man be speaking rightly? “No, venerable sir. For what reason? Because the great earth is vast, venerable sir, and the grain of dust on the tip of the fingernail is trifling; the great earth is the greater, and the grain of dust on the tip of the fingernail is the lesser. “It is in such a way, bhikkhus, that one who possesses right view regarding these five aggregates subject to clinging speaks rightly. What five? Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. It is in such a way, bhikkhus, that one who possesses right view regarding these five aggregates subject to clinging speaks rightly. “Suppose, bhikkhus, a man were to take up a single drop of water from the tip of a blade of grass and say: ‘The great ocean is as much as this drop of water on the tip of the blade of grass, and not more. Now, bhikkhus, would that man be speaking rightly? “No, venerable sir. For what reason? Because the great ocean is vast, venerable sir, and the drop of water on the tip of the blade of grass is trifling; the great ocean is the greater, and the drop of water on the tip of the blade of grass is the lesser. “It is in such a way, bhikkhus, that one who possesses right view regarding these five aggregates subject to clinging speaks rightly. What five? Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’... ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. It is in such a way, bhikkhus, that one who possesses right view regarding these five aggregates subject to clinging speaks rightly. “Suppose, bhikkhus, a man were to take up a single mote of dust from the tip of a fingernail and say: ‘The great earth is as much as this mote of dust on the tip of my fingernail, and not more. Now, bhikkhus, would that man be speaking rightly? “No, venerable sir. For what reason? Because the great earth is vast, venerable sir, and the mote of dust on the tip of the fingernail is trifling; the great earth is the greater, and the mote of dust on the tip of the fingernail is the lesser. “It is in such a way, bhikkhus, that one who possesses right view regarding these five aggregates subject to clinging speaks rightly. It is in such a way, bhikkhus, that one who possesses right view regarding these five aggregates subject to clinging speaks rightly. “Suppose, bhikkhus, a man were to take up a single drop of water from the tip of a blade of grass and say: ‘The great ocean is as much as this drop of water on the tip of the blade of grass, and not more. Because the great ocean is vast, venerable sir, and the drop of water on the tip of the blade of grass is trifling; the great ocean is the greater, and the drop of water on the tip of the blade of grass is the lesser.

The Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī.
Then the Blessed One, having placed a small amount of dust on the tip of his fingernail, addressed the bhikkhus:
“What do you think, bhikkhus?”
“Which, then, is more: this small amount of dust that I have placed on the tip of my fingernail, or this great earth?
“Venerable sir, this great earth alone is more;
the small amount of dust placed by the Blessed One on the tip of his fingernail is trifling.”

“Compared to the great earth, the amount of dust placed on the tip of a fingernail by the Blessed One does not approach it in number, does not approach it in comparison, nor does it even approach a fraction of it.
“In the same way, bhikkhus, those beings who are reborn among humans are few;
rather, those beings who are reborn elsewhere than among humans are far more numerous.”
"Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus:
‘We shall dwell heedfully.
It is in this way, bhikkhus, that you should train yourselves."
The Second [Discourse]. Saṃyutta Nikāya 20.3 (SN 20.3, PTS SN ii 263) 1.
The Chapter on Similes (Opammavagga)
The Kula Sutta.
At Sāvatthī, the Blessed One was staying.
“Bhikkhus, just as those families that have many women and few men are easily plundered by thieves and bandits;”
"In the same way, monks, whichever monk has not developed and cultivated the liberation of mind through loving-kindness is easily overcome by non-human beings.
Just as those families, monks, that have few women and many men are difficult for thieves and bandits to overpower,
even so, monks, whichever monk has developed and cultivated the liberation of mind through loving-kindness is difficult for non-human beings to overpower."
"Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
'The liberation of mind that is loving-kindness shall be developed by us, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, consolidated, and well undertaken.
It is in this way, monks, that you should train yourselves."
Third.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 20.4 (SN 20.4, PTS SN ii 264) 1.
Opamma-vagga (The Chapter on Similes)
The Okkhā Sutta.
At Sāvatthī, the Blessed One was staying there.
"Bhikkhus, if someone were to give a gift of a hundred okkhā fruits in the morning, and if someone else were to give a gift of a hundred okkhā fruits at midday..."
One might give a gift; one might give a gift of a hundred pots of boiled rice in the evening;

or one might develop a mind of loving-kindness for as little as the time it takes to milk a cow in the morning; or one might develop a mind of loving-kindness for as little as the time it takes to milk a cow at midday;
or one might develop a mind of loving-kindness for as little as the time it takes to milk a cow in the evening.
One should develop a mind of loving-kindness; this yields far more abundant fruit than that.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
‘Our liberation of mind through loving-kindness will be developed, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, consolidated, and well undertaken.’”
“In this way, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves.
The fourth.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 20.5 (SN 20.5, PTS SN ii 265)
1. The Chapter on Similes:
The Discourse on the Spear. At Sāvatthī, the Blessed One was staying.
“Bhikkhus, it is just as if there were a spear with a sharp blade.
Then a man might come along thinking:
‘I will grasp this spear with its sharp blade with my hand or my fist; I will rub it back and forth; I will twist it around.’”
“What do you think, monks,
would that man be able to take hold of that sharp-edged spear with his hand or fist, to strike it back, or to turn it aside?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“And for what reason?
“Because that spear with its sharp point, venerable sir, would not be easy to grasp with the hand or the fist, nor to strike back at, nor to twist away;
moreover, that man would simply partake of exhaustion and distress.”
“In the same way, monks, if any monk has developed and cultivated the liberation of mind through loving-kindness—
made it his vehicle, made it his foundation, established it, consolidated it, and properly undertaken it— and if a non-human being should think to disturb his mind,
then that very non-human being would be the one to suffer exhaustion and frustration.”
"Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
'The liberation of mind through loving-kindness shall be developed by us, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, consolidated, and well undertaken.
It is in this way, monks, that you should train yourselves."
The Fifth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 20.6 (SN 20.6, PTS SN ii 265) 1.
The Chapter on Similes (Opammavagga)
The Discourse on the Archers. At Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, suppose there were four archers of firm strength, well-trained, skilled of hand, and practiced in their craft, standing in the four directions.”
Then, suppose a man were to come along saying:
"I shall go and retrieve the four arrows shot in the four directions by these four firm-bowed archers who are well-trained, skilled, and experienced, before they have even touched the ground.
What do you think, monks?
“Is it sufficient to say, ‘A man is swift, endowed with supreme speed’?

“If, venerable sir, one were to catch an arrow shot by a single firm-bowed archer—one who is well-trained, skilled of hand, and practiced—and bring it back before it has even touched the ground, that would be sufficient to say, ‘A man is swift, endowed with supreme speed.
How much more so, then, for four such firm-bowed archers, well-trained, skilled of hand, and practiced?”
“Monks, the speed of that man is swifter than the speed of the sun and moon;
and, monks, the speed of that man, the speed of the sun and moon,
and the speed of those deities who run before the sun and moon— [all] are swifter than that.”
The formations of life are wasting away.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
"We shall dwell heedfully."
“In this way, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves.
The sixth.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 20.7 (SN 20.7, PTS SN ii 266)
1. The Chapter on Similes:
The Discourse on the Axle. At Sāvatthī, [the Blessed One] was dwelling.
“Once upon a time, monks, the Dasārhas had a drum named Ānaka.
When that Ānaka was struck, the Dasārhas inserted another peg.
There came a time, monks, when the old lotus-shaped head of the Ānaka drum disappeared.”
Only the outer robe remained. In the same way, monks, in the future there will be monks who, when those discourses spoken by the Tathāgata—
which are profound, of profound meaning, transcendent, and connected with emptiness— are being recited, will not wish to listen.
They will not lend an ear, nor will they apply their minds toward understanding,
nor will they consider those teachings as something to be learned or mastered.
Furthermore, as for those discourses that are merely poetic fabrications— verses composed in poetic style, with elegant syllables and refined phrasing, being external and spoken by disciples—
When these are being recited, they will wish to hear them, they will lend an ear, they will apply their minds to understanding,
and they will consider those teachings as something to be mastered and thoroughly learned.
In this way, monks, there will be the disappearance of these discourses spoken by the Tathāgata— profound, with profound meaning, supramundane, and connected with emptiness.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
"When those discourses spoken by the Tathāgata—which are profound, profound in meaning, transcendent, and connected with emptiness—are being recited, we will desire to hear them;
we will lend an ear; we will apply our minds to full understanding."
‘We shall learn and master the Dhamma.
It is in this way, monks, that you should train yourselves.
This is the seventh [sutta].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 20.8 (SN 20.8, PTS SN ii 267) 1. Opamma-vagga Kaliṅgara Sutta: The Log “Bhikkhus, suppose a man were to throw a log of wood into a river that was flowing along swiftly. And suppose that log were to be carried away by the current, not drifting toward either bank, nor grounded on a sandbank, nor seized by a crocodile, nor caught in a whirlpool, nor fouled by moss. That log would simply go on to the great ocean. In the same way, bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu does not associate with sense pleasures, does not associate with unwholesome states, does not associate with evil, unwholesome qualities, and does not associate with the company of householders or those gone forth, he will simply go on to the great ocean of liberation. Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We shall not associate with sense pleasures… we shall not associate with the company of householders or those gone forth. Thus, bhikkhus, should you train yourselves.”
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Gabled Hall.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Monks,” [the Blessed One said]. “Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One spoke as follows:
“Monks, at present the Licchavis dwell wearing armor; they are diligent and ardent in their practice.
Against them, Ajātasattu Vedehiputta, the King of Magadha, finds no opening and finds no foothold.
Monks, in the future there will be Licchavis who are delicate, with hands and feet that are soft and tender.”
They will lie down on soft beds with cotton pillows until the rising of the sun.
King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha will find an opportunity and find a pretext against them.
But now, monks, the bhikkhus dwell with their limbs as supports, heedful, ardent, and resolute in their striving.
Māra the Evil One finds no opportunity and finds no foothold against them.
Monks, in the future there will be monks who are delicate, with hands and feet that are soft and tender.
They will spend their nights on soft beds with cotton pillows until the rising of the sun.
Māra the Evil One will find an opportunity and find a foothold against them.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
"We shall dwell with a boulder as our pillow, heedful, ardent, and resolute in our striving."
“In this way, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves.
The eighth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 20.9 (SN 20.9, PTS SN ii 268)
1. The Chapter on Similes:
The Discourse on the Elephant Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, a certain newly ordained bhikkhu was visiting families excessively.
The bhikkhus said this to him:
“Venerable sir, do not visit families excessively.
When that bhikkhu was addressed by the bhikkhus in this way, he said:
“If even these elder bhikkhus think that families should be visited, how much more so should I?”

Then a number of bhikkhus approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. As they were sitting there, those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, here a certain newly ordained bhikkhu visits families excessively.
Regarding him, the bhikkhus say this:”
‘Venerable sir, do not visit families excessively.
When that bhikkhu was spoken to by the bhikkhus, he said this:
‘If even these elder bhikkhus think that families should be visited, how much more so should I?’”
“Once upon a time, monks, there was a great lake in a forest region.
Elephants lived depending on that lake.
Having plunged into the lake, they would pull up lotus roots and stalks with their trunks, rinse them thoroughly until they were free of mud, chew them, and swallow them.
That [lotus root] serves both for their beauty and for their strength, yet they do not meet death or suffering amounting to death on that account.
Now, monks, young elephant calves, training after those very great elephants, enter that lake,
pull up lotus roots and stalks with their trunks, and instead of rinsing them well, rinse them while they are still muddy.
They swallow it without chewing it.
That food serves neither for their beauty nor for their strength;
on that account, they meet with death or with suffering amounting to death.
In the same way, monks, here elder bhikkhus, having dressed in the morning and taken their bowls and robes, enter a village or town for alms.
There they speak the Dhamma,
and the householders show them signs of faith.
They enjoy those gains without being attached, infatuated, or obsessed with them; seeing the danger and possessing the wisdom of escape, they consume them.
This serves for their beauty and strength, and because of it, they do not meet death or suffering amounting to death.
Now, monks, junior bhikkhus who are training under those elder bhikkhus, having dressed in the morning and taken their bowls and robes, enter a village or town for alms.
They preach the Dhamma there.
The householders show them signs of faith.
They consume those gains, being greedy for them, infatuated with them, and obsessed by them; they do not see the danger in them and lack the wisdom regarding the escape from them.
That does not lead to their welfare or strength; on that account, they meet death or suffering amounting to death.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
"Unattached, uninfatuated, and not clinging, seeing the danger and possessing the wisdom of escape, we shall make use of those gains."
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
Thus [ends] the ninth [discourse]. Saṁyutta Nikāya 20.10 (SN 20.10, PTS SN ii 270).
1. The Chapter on Similes:
The Cat Discourse.
At Sāvatthī, [the Blessed One] was dwelling.
Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu was visiting families excessively.
The bhikkhus said to him:
"Venerable sir, do not visit families excessively."
Thus, when that bhikkhu was being spoken to by the bhikkhus, he did not desist.
Then a number of bhikkhus approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. Sitting there, those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, here a certain bhikkhu is excessively frequenting families.”
The monks said to him:
“Venerable sir, do not go on visiting families at such excessive times.
Though being spoken to by the monks in this way, that monk did not desist.
“Once upon a time, monks, a cat was standing at a junction where there was a narrow passage, seeking a soft mouse, thinking:
‘When this soft mouse goes out for its prey, I shall catch it right there and eat it.
Then, monks, that soft mouse went out for its prey.”
The cat seized him, devoured him hastily, and swallowed him down.
That soft mouse ate even his intestines and ate his intestinal coils as well.
Because of that, he met with death or suffering equal to death.
In the same way, monks, here a certain monk, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe,
enters a village or town for alms with body unguarded, speech unguarded, mind unguarded,
with mindfulness unestablished, and the sense faculties unrestrained.
Thereupon, he sees a woman poorly dressed or poorly clad.
Having seen that woman poorly dressed or poorly clad, lust invades his mind.
With a mind invaded by lust, he meets with death or with suffering amounting to death.
For in the discipline of the Noble One, monks, this is death: when one who has undertaken the training abandons it and reverts to the low life.
This too, monks, is suffering as great as death: namely, when one falls into some defiled offense for which a means of rehabilitation is prescribed.
"Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
'With body guarded, speech guarded, mind guarded, with mindfulness established, and with the sense faculties restrained, we shall enter a village or town for alms.
It is in this way, monks, that you should train yourselves."
The Tenth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 20.11 (SN 20.11, PTS SN ii 271) 1.
The Chapter on Similes (Opammavagga)
The Discourse to the Jackal. At Sāvatthī, the Blessed One was staying.
“Bhikkhus, have you heard the sound of an old jackal howling at the time of dawn? “Have you not heard, bhikkhus, the sound of an old jackal howling at the time of dawn?”
“Yes, venerable sir.
“This old jackal, monks, was afflicted by a disease called *ukkaṇḍaka*.
He goes wherever he wishes;”
Wherever he wishes, there he stands;
wherever he wishes, there he sits;
wherever he wishes, there he lies down.
Even a cool breeze blows upon him.
It would be well, monks, if someone here claiming to be a follower of the Sakyan son were to experience such an acquisition of a personal existence.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
‘We shall dwell heedfully.
In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
Thus ends the eleventh [sutta].

Saṁyutta Nikāya 20.12 (SN 20.12, PTS SN ii 272) 1. Opammavagga The Second Jackal Sutta At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, suppose a jackal, while wandering in search of food at night in a charnel ground, were to catch sight of a human corpse, half-eaten by crows, half-eaten by vultures, half-eaten by dogs, half-eaten by jackals, half-eaten by various kinds of worms, and smeared with blood. Then a second jackal would come along, desiring what that first one desires, seeking what that one seeks, longing for what that one longs for. Seeing the first jackal, it would say: ‘What on earth are you doing, friend? Why do you stand there, frightened, terrified, and full of fear? “Then the first jackal would say to the second: ‘Friend, this is a human corpse, half-eaten by crows, half-eaten by vultures, half-eaten by dogs, half-eaten by jackals, half-eaten by various kinds of worms, and smeared with blood. I am not afraid of it, nor terrified of it, nor full of fear because of it. “Then the second jackal would say to the first: ‘But, friend, I too am not afraid of it, nor terrified of it, nor full of fear because of it. Come, let us both eat it together. And the two jackals would eat that human corpse, half-eaten by crows, half-eaten by vultures, half-eaten by dogs, half-eaten by jackals, half-eaten by various kinds of worms, and smeared with blood. “Then a third jackal would come along... [as before] ...And the three jackals would eat that human corpse... “Then a fourth jackal would come along... [as before] ...And the four jackals would eat that human corpse... “Then a fifth jackal would come along... [as before] ...And the five jackals would eat that human corpse... “Then a sixth jackal would come along... [as before] ...And the six jackals would eat that human corpse... “Then a seventh jackal would come along... [as before] ...And the seven jackals would eat that human corpse, half-eaten by crows, half-eaten by vultures, half-eaten by dogs, half-eaten by jackals, half-eaten by various kinds of worms, and smeared with blood. “Now, bhikkhus, what do you think? Would those jackals eat that human corpse out of greed, or out of hatred, or out of delusion? “Venerable sir, those jackals would eat that human corpse out of greed, not out of hatred, nor out of delusion. “It is just as well, bhikkhus, that you understand this matter thus. For those who, when I speak in such a way, understand me to be teaching the abandoning of greed, hatred, and delusion—they truly understand my teaching. But those who, when I speak in such a way, understand me to be teaching the cultivation of greed, hatred, and delusion—they do not truly understand my teaching. “Bhikkhus, I have taught the abandoning of greed, hatred, and delusion; I have taught the path leading to the abandoning of greed, hatred, and delusion. Whatever ascetics and brahmins in the past have correctly awakened to things as they really are, all have done so by abandoning greed, hatred, and delusion, and by developing the path leading to the abandoning of greed, hatred, and delusion. Whatever ascetics and brahmins in the future will correctly awaken to things as they really are, all will do so by abandoning greed, hatred, and delusion, and by developing the path leading to the abandoning of greed, hatred, and delusion. Whatever ascetics and brahmins at present have correctly awakened to things as they really are, all have done so by abandoning greed, hatred, and delusion, and by developing the path leading to the abandoning of greed, hatred, and delusion. “Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We shall abandon greed, hatred, and delusion, and we shall develop the path leading to the abandoning of greed, hatred, and delusion. It is in such a way that you should train yourselves.”
Staying at Sāvatthī, [the Blessed One said]:
“Bhikkhus, did you hear last night, at the time of dawn, an old jackal howling?
“Yes, venerable sir.”
“Bhikkhus, there might be some gratitude and thankfulness in that old jackal, yet there would be no gratitude or thankfulness whatsoever among those here who claim to be followers of the Sakyan son.
Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus:
‘We shall be grateful and thankful.’”
"Furthermore, nothing even as small as we have done for one another shall go to waste.
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
Thus ends the twelfth [discourse].
The First Chapter on Similes.
Its summary verse:
The peak, the fingernail-tip, and the family.
The well, the spear, the archer;
the wedge, the log, the elephant;
the cat, and two jackals.
The Connected Discourses on Similes is complete.
